extracted.intended_audience: readers and critics of literature, culture, and social philosophy; writers and intellectuals interested in standards of taste and moral evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and critical criteria for judging modern thinkers, writers, utopias, scientific attitudes, and religious movements—focusing on humility, wonder, realism about human nature, and moral measures of greatness. The page offers examples and counterexamples (Shaw, Wells, Darwin, Salvation Army, Utopias) to illustrate evaluative norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to wonder / expectation of surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Blessed is he that expecteth nothing, for he shall be gloriously surprised — genuine appreciation requires expecting nothing and therefore being open to surprising, prodigious aspects of ordinary life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton contrasts the capacity to see 'the incredible unexpectedness of a fairy-tale' in ordinary faces with the habit of 'pedantic and fastidious comparisons' that deaden wonder. Example/anti-pattern: Shaw is critiqued for not being easily pleased; the properly appreciative person sees redder roses and greener grass because they expect nothing. Verbosity: emphasizes psychological disposition rather than technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility as source of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine appreciation and the capacity for great deeds rest on humility — a 'mystery of humility and almost of darkness' that enables adventure and romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton argues humility releases the soul for 'incredible voyages' and unmerited triumphs; humility often appears as worldly success (scarlet and gold) yet remains essentially humble. Anti-pattern: mistaking humility for vice or mere vanity; failing to value smallness. Examples: Christian humility producing Romance; Darwin's unconscious humility making him convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small things please great minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Great minds are pleased by little things; an appreciation of trivial or humble aspects is a mark of greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim opposes the idea that greatness despises smallness. Chesterton uses the example of Christ choosing a 'shuffler, a snob a coward' (Peter) as the foundation of the Church — showing value in weakness and smallness. Anti-pattern: throwing away humanity for 'progress' (Shaw's proposed new man).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific humility (unconsciousness) as moral and intellectual virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The man of science's humility — a kind of ingenuous unconsciousness about the cosmic effects of his work — is a strength that made great scientists persuasive and powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton praises scientists who treated monumental discoveries as by-products of their quiet pursuits (Darwin, early savants). Anti-patterns: scientists becoming 'aesthetic' about their discoveries, proud of their humility, which weakens their position (contrast Huxley vs Darwin). Example: Darwin had 'no answer possible' because of his unconsciousness; Huxley had answers because of pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty shown by intellectual growth toward the ordinary
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's honesty is evidenced when their development is a steady advance from startling opinions toward more conventional or humdrum views, not fickle theatrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton identifies Wells's move from sensational theories to more conventional beliefs as evidence of his honesty and non-poseur character. Anti-pattern: perpetual leaping from one position to another (e.g., George Moore) which suggests vanity or insincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate greatness by moral usefulness, not merely by power or size
rubrics_metrics.description: A being must be tested against human standards (religion, politics, duties) — mere force, size, or novelty does not establish greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton argues the Superman or giant must 'submit to our test' — e.g., is he fond of children, what are his political views, is his heart in the right place. Giants who do not conform to human standards remain 'vermin.' Example: 'Jack the Giant-Killer' judges the giant by usefulness to humans. Anti-pattern: hero-worship of mere strength (Nietzsche, some Shawites).

rubrics_metrics.name: A common standard is necessary for 'surpassing' to be meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: To say something 'surpasses' us presupposes a shared standard; greatness implies conformity to some human measure, otherwise superiority is meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton invokes Nietzsche's phrase 'Man is a thing which has to be surpassed' to show that 'surpass' implies a standard common to both. Anti-pattern: declaring supermen who do not meet human standards to be superior merely by other metrics (e.g., size).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroism defined by sensibility and increased feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: True heroism is being more human — having greater sensibility and capacity to feel (Achilles) — not being cold, detached, or 'friendless' as Nietzsche's Superman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton contrasts Achilles (who feels deeply) with Nietzsche's Superman ('be hard' = 'be dead'). The criterion values 'sensibility' as the definition of life and heroic greatness. Anti-pattern: valorizing hardness or emotional sterility as virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value the weak as the school of courage (sympathy with the small)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathy for the small or defeated is not sentimentalism but the 'first law of practical courage' — to be in the weakest camp trains the strongest character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton contends that being weak fosters bravery and practical strength; historical ballads praise the weak-defeating-strong. Anti-pattern: exclusive admiration of strength leading to misplaced hero-worship of Caesars and Supermen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism about human nature in utopian proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Utopias are flawed if they begin by assuming that the greatest human difficulties (selfishness, original sin) are solved; they must begin with the human soul and material realities of people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton criticizes Wells's Utopia for disbelieving in original sin and for starting with protoplasm rather than the soul. Anti-pattern: designing systems that assume humans won't want more than their share or that human selfishness is gone. Examples: scientific marriage proposals; world-state cosmopolitanism that ignores enduring patriotic/differentiating impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for differentiation and conflicting ideals in political design
rubrics_metrics.description: Political and social designs must recognize that the highest things tend to produce differentiation and conflict of ideals; a world-state will not erase causes for war or strife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton argues varieties in art, opinion, and government are inevitable; preventing union doesn't prevent differentiation-driven conflict. Example: even in a world-state, different Utopias would fight. Anti-pattern: believing a single global system removes deeper conflicts of ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between mutable manifestations and immutable ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Change in manifest things does not imply absence of unchangeable abstract qualities; knowledge requires some abiding commonality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton critiques Wells's relativism: saying 'there is no being, but a universal becoming' ignores paradox that difference implies similarity. Example: the idea of light remains even as relative intensities vary. Anti-pattern: radical relativism that denies any stable concept and thus undermines knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge religious movements by their visible methods and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: While the aims of a religious movement may be hard to judge, its methods (ritual, popular forms) are easily assessable and may be spiritually effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton defends the Salvation Army's brass bands and sensational ritual as the 'old voice of glad and angry faith' — a valid spiritual expression. Anti-pattern: dismissing popular or military-like religious methods as vulgar without recognizing their genuine spiritual function. Note: separates sociological efficacy (aims) from immediate ritual impact (methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of undifferentiated syncretism (mixing creeds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting the 'beautiful' parts of many creeds without discerning which parts are genuinely good can produce a muddled, inferior blend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton warns that undenominational religions risk taking the dull parts from each and producing 'mud.' The evaluator must detect which parts of a creed are genuinely good vs bad before synthesizing. Anti-pattern: assuming that mixing all 'beautiful' bits will yield purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health and human practices should originate in natural pleasure, not precaution
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental human functions (eating, exercise, marriage) should be performed for pleasure, not as duties carried out from medical precaution or utilitarian calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton argues that health has to do with carelessness and that trying to make marriage or exercise purely instrumental undermines them. Anti-pattern: medicalized social engineering (e.g., breeding humans like animals) that ignores love and natural excitement. Example: critique of 'scientific marriage' proponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utopian schemes must not assume eradication of the hardest human problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief defect of Utopias is assuming the greatest difficulty (selfishness, desire for more) is already overcome and then detailing solutions to minor problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton notes Utopias typically 'take the greatest difficulty of man and assume it to be overcome' and then plan for delivery mechanisms (motor-car vs balloon). Anti-pattern: blueprints that ignore innate tendencies toward wanting more or seeking differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate continuity and direction in intellectual development
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress should be understood as having a definable direction (not arbitrary shifts); change presupposes some fixed notion of quality or property (the 'North Pole' analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton argues that while progress may vary, the direction must be firm enough to map smaller regions (we can map Brighton because the North Pole is definable). Anti-pattern: nihilistic relativism that treats all change as undirected and denies usable standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate writers and ideas by their practical consequences and fidelity to human realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical judgment should focus on whether ideas and literary works serve human needs, reflect human psychology, and yield moral and social consequences consistent with human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the essay Chesterton uses practical tests: does an idea make men better (fond of children, citizens dutiful), does it respect human psychology, does it prepare for 'trophies of His ancient war' (spiritual goods). Anti-pattern: abstract theorizing that ignores ordinary human psychology and leads to destructive policies or aesthetic postures.
